chapter_theme: In the court of the lion throne the poets praise the king, an astrologer is admitted and reads a night's dream as the coming of a Vidyadhara king's daughter and a messenger with a letter, the court affirms it and names Tivittan, and in the council hall the ministers speak of his lordship of the discus and plan a guarded garden for the day.

cast.role: the reigning king on the lion throne (Prajapati by tradition)
the young lord of the dream, named at 109
the king's counsellors, who give counsel in the council hall
the kings who attend the court
the poets who sing the king's praise
the astrologer who reads the dream
the guard posted in the garden

95.reading: The throne is described, with a fanged beast carved on it gripping an elephant calf, and the lord who takes his seat on it is likened to the fierce sun spreading over the top of the rising hill.
95.event: The lord takes his seat on the lion throne.

96.reading: The priest, the garlanded counsellors and the kings of the sea-like army take the places assigned to them, watching the sign of the lord and at the order of the lotus-eyed one.
96.nuance: இறைமகன் (line 3) and தாமரைச் செங்கண் தம்மான் (line 4) are not named; they may be one person, the prince, or the lord on the throne, so who sets the seating is not fixed here.
96.event: Priest, counsellors and kings take their appointed seats at the lord's sign.

97.reading: After the elder one is seated, the victorious kings touch their crowns to the king's anklets and take the places that the younger one assigns them in due order.
97.nuance: முன்னவர் and பின்னவன் are not named; they read as the elder and younger prince, and the younger is likely Tivittan, who is named at 109, but the verse does not say so.
97.event: The kings bow their crowned heads at the king's feet and take the seats the younger prince assigns.

98.reading: Men of hereditary line, loving the king's feet, proud in victory and strong of arm, are what the king of the frontleted war-elephant keeps at his side.
98.nuance: இளையவர் (line 3) may mean young warriors or the younger princes; the sentence is read as describing the king's attendants.
98.event: The king places loyal men of old families beside him as attendants.

99.reading: When the king stands in full bloom like a golden wishing tree, the poets, like bees, gather to his bright face and begin to sing in measured melody.
99.event: The poets gather and begin to sing the king's praise.

100.reading: The poets, skilled in the books of the lute and song, sing that the king's fame fills the earth, and wish long life to the feet that guard the world under the moon-like white umbrella.
100.event: The poets sing and wish the king long life.

101.reading: The poets praise the king as the one who rose from a line guarded by a bright god, who turned rival kings' eyes away with one fierce spear, and bid his rule go on.
101.nuance: The verse credits the line's survival to a god of bright lustre; who is meant is not named.

102.reading: The king, seated among the praise, tells the doorkeeper to lift the guard and let in whoever comes until seven nazhikai have passed.
102.nuance: காவல் வரவிடு can mean opening the gate or letting the guard down; either way the order is that the court is open to any caller for seven nazhikai.
102.event: The king orders the doorkeeper to admit anyone for seven nazhikai.

103.reading: A learned astrologer, who knows by thought what happens far off, tells the doorkeeper that if he finds an opening he would see the king, and bids the man judge the moment.
103.nuance: Line 1 அலகின் மெய்ந்நூல் அபவு சென்று is obscure; the sense that he is a master of an exact science and waits at the gate is clear.
103.event: The astrologer asks the doorkeeper whether he may see the king.

claims.claim: one trained in the exact science knows what happens far away by thought

104.reading: The doorkeeper, knowing the king's mind, tells the astrologer he has leave to enter; the king, a white flower in his hand, shows him a high seat and bids him sit at ease.
104.event: The doorkeeper admits the astrologer and the king offers him a seat.

105.reading: Having laid aside worldly courtesies as his discipline asks, the astrologer, who has looked fully at the three times, waits for the king's sign and then speaks, wishing to show the mastery of the books he has learned.
105.nuance: The narrator gives his motive as showing his learning (line 4), which colours the prophecy that follows; Naladiyar 52 treats the study of astrology as folly.
105.event: The astrologer, after waiting on the king's sign, begins to speak.

claims.claim: a man learned in the books can see all three times, past, present and to come

106.reading: The astrologer tells the king that a dream was seen in the night: an elephant came down from the sky, set a shining garland of white flowers on the sea-hued young lord, and went to its own place.
106.nuance: The Tamil does not say whose dream; 111 suggests the king's. The identification of the sea-hued young lord with Tivittan rests on 109.
106.event: The astrologer relates the night's dream of the sky-descending elephant that garlands the young lord.

107.reading: The astrologer gives the dream's fruit: a Vidyadhara king in shining jewels will come, praise the young lord's name, give him one of his daughters and go.
107.event: The astrologer foretells that a Vidyadhara king will give his daughter to the young lord.

claims.claim: a dream of an elephant garlanding a youth foretells a bride given by a king of the Vidyadharas

108.reading: The astrologer adds that when seven have passed, a man able to speak well will come down with a letter into the garden called Pushpakarandam.
108.nuance: நானேளு (line 2) looks like a misprint for நா னேழு; the unit of seven is not named and may be the seven nazhikai of 102.
108.event: The astrologer foretells the arrival of a messenger with a letter in the Pushpakarandam garden.

claims.claim: a messenger with a letter will descend into the Pushpakarandam garden after seven have passed

109.reading: Those seated marvel and answer that Tivittan is indeed of this kind, the one who will protect the whole joined world under one umbrella, and say the prophecy is not false.
109.nuance: The vocative in lines 3-4 addresses the one who will rule under one umbrella, and the court is taken to speak of Tivittan; they confirm the astrologer without any test.
109.event: The assembly names Tivittan as the one foretold and affirms the prophecy.

claims.claim: Tivittan will guard the whole world under a single umbrella

110.reading: After about one nazhikai a drum sounds; the king dismisses the court with a look, turns to his counsellors and goes to the council hall of his tall mansion.
110.nuance: அகத்தநூலவர் is read as those learned in the counsel-books, the ministers (compare மந்திரத்துளார் in 113).
110.event: The king ends the audience and withdraws to the council hall with his counsellors.

111.reading: In the council hall the king recounts the night's dream as the astrologer interpreted it and the fortunate fruit he assigned, and lifts his crowned head.
111.nuance: தூக்கினான் is read as raising his head; it could also mean weighing the matter.
111.event: The king repeats the dream and its fruit to his ministers.

112.reading: The ministers answer the king that he whom the whole encircled world will worship and lie down in the shade of will bloom as lord of the discus, which they had heard before.
112.nuance: பண்டுங் கேட்டுமே says they had heard this before; an earlier prophecy about the prince is not shown here.

claims.claim: the one before whom the whole world bows will become lord of the discus, a universal ruler

113.reading: The ministers, knowing the king's mind and saying the young lord must have good austerity, begin their counsel.
113.nuance: The verse does not say that the austerity was of a past birth, and no school's doctrine of merit is named.
113.event: The ministers begin to give counsel.

claims.claim: the young lord's rising fortune comes from good austerity

114.reading: The ministers say that the conch-line and the discus-line are on the young lord's palm, so he will hold the discus weapon in his hand like the conch-handed lord.
114.nuance: The comparison borrows the image of Vishnu, the conch-handed; the verse does not call the prince Vishnu.

claims.claim: conch and discus lines on the palm show a man who will wield the discus

115.reading: The ministers say that if the Vidyadhara king's slender, peacock-gaited daughter comes down without fail, the rule of that world will follow.
115.nuance: Line 4 அஞ்சிநின் றவ்வுலகாட்சி செல்லுமே is hard to construe; the sense that the Vidyadhara realm's rule is tied to the bride's descent is not certain.

116.reading: The ministers propose that, for the day the astrologer named, they set the fragrant stone platform in order and post Turumakanthan as guard in the lovely garden.
116.event: The ministers propose to prepare the stone platform and set Turumakanthan to guard the garden.

117.reading: The king approves the plan as very good, orders Turumakanthan to go and guard daily, and goes to the palace of his dear consorts.
117.nuance: இன்றுணையவர் கடங் கோயில் is read as the palace of his consorts.
117.event: The king approves the plan, charges the guard and goes to the consorts' palace.

118.reading: Turumakanthan bows at the king's feet and goes to the flower garden where bees hum and honey drips from the long branches.
118.event: Turumakanthan goes to the garden to keep watch.

links.note: The astrologer waits on the king's sign and then speaks to show his learning, with a sight of all three times; Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle of the stars the most foolish of the foolish, set against the thought of death.
links.teaches: The story rests its plot on an astrologer who is admitted, heard and believed by the whole court, while the quatrain calls his craft folly, so the two give opposite verdicts on the same trade.

gains.a: The poem's own motive line, that he speaks to display his learning, gets an outside judgment on whether that learning is worth the court's trust.
gains.b: The quatrain's charge of folly meets an astrologer who is welcomed by a king, which shows the claim being tested against a trusted practitioner.

links.note: The astrologer sets aside courtesies, waits for the king's sign and speaks; Kural 696 tells a speaker to know the mood, weigh the time and say what is wanted and not disliked.
links.teaches: The astrologer keeps the Kural's rule of reading the king and timing his speech, but the poet names his aim as showing his learning, a motive the couplet never allows for.

gains.a: The wait for the king's sign is given a stated rule behind it, so it reads as court craft and not mere delay.
gains.b: The couplet's advice is shown in a scene where the speaker has something the king will welcome, and where the speaker's vanity can still sit under a correct manner.

links.note: Kannaki's dream of trouble in Madurai, told to Kovalan before he leaves, and the astrologer's dream of an elephant garlanding the young lord are both dreams that foretell what is to come.
links.teaches: In the Silappathikaram the dream is a warning that cannot turn the course of fate, while here it is a promise that the court at once turns into a plan, so one image serves ruin in one epic and fortune in the other.

links.note: The astrologer reads a night's dream as true knowledge of what will come; the Siddhar song says all he saw has turned into a dream, like moonlight on a forest.
links.teaches: One poem trusts a dream to show what is real in the future, and the other uses the dream as the name for the whole of what is seen, so the same word divides prophecy from unreality.

gains.a: The prophetic dream gets a view that holds waking sight itself to be dream-like, which unsettles the court's easy trust in the sign.
gains.b: The Siddhar's figure of dream as unreality meets a dream treated as sure foreknowledge, which shows what the figure is set against.

links.note: Verse 106 gives the dream of the elephant that garlands the young lord; 107 gives its fruit, a Vidyadhara king's gift of his daughter.
links.teaches: The astrologer first tells the dream and only then its fruit, so the reader sees a sign turned into a forecast of a marriage and an alliance.

links.note: The astrologer foretells a messenger with a letter in the Pushpakarandam garden; the ministers propose to set the stone platform in order and post a guard in the garden on his day.
links.teaches: The court does not wait on the prophecy but prepares the place it names, so counsel here means arranging the ground for a sign the king has only just heard.

links.note: The ministers propose to place Turumakanthan as guard in the garden; he goes to the garden after bowing to the king.
links.teaches: The proposal becomes action in two verses, and the guard sets out only after the king's approval, which shows how a counsel becomes an order.

source_issues: 108 line 2 நானேளு looks like a misprint for நா னேழு; the unit counted is not named.
103 line 1 அலகின் மெய்ந்நூல் அபவு சென்று is obscure.
115 line 4 அஞ்சிநின் றவ்வுலகாட்சி செல்லுமே is hard to construe.
